Newborn Cape gerbils emerge into the world at a remarkably modest size, weighing only 4.5 grams [Wwb = 4.5 grams]. This altricial neonate is entirely dependent on maternal care, and its small birth mass places it on the lower end of the spectrum among related murid rodents. The initial period of life is dominated by a rapid phase of mass gain, fueled entirely by the mother's rich milk during the suckling juvenile stage. Under controlled captive conditions maintained at 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], the nutritional independence of the pups is achieved relatively quickly; the time since birth at weaning is a brief 23 days [tx = 23 days]. This short pre-weaning interval suggests a high maternal investment efficiency, allowing the female to redirect her energy towards subsequent reproductive efforts without an extended period of lactation. The transition from milk to solid food marks a critical milestone, as the young must quickly develop the foraging skills necessary to process the seeds and arthropods that constitute the adult diet. This rapid weaning age is a key life-history adaptation for a species inhabiting the unpredictable, seasonal environments of the South African fynbos and karoo, where favorable conditions for offspring survival can be fleeting.

Following the weaning milestone, the young Cape gerbils enter a juvenile period characterized by continued somatic growth and the development of adult behaviors. This pre-reproductive phase is a critical window during which individuals must accumulate sufficient body reserves to support the energetic demands of future reproduction. Sexual maturation, a pivotal developmental transition, typically occurs at 152 days [tp = 152 days] after birth under standard laboratory conditions kept at 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. This age at puberty is a relatively extended duration for a small mammal, suggesting a strategic delay that allows individuals to reach a more competitive body size before engaging in the high-stakes activity of breeding. For females, the acquisition of a large adult frame is particularly important, as body size is often a strong predictor of litter size and offspring survival. Reaching this reproductive threshold represents a major energetic investment, and the date of first estrus typically follows soon after, marking the onset of the animal's reproductive career within the population.

The reproductive biology of the Cape gerbil is finely tuned to maximize output during favorable periods. A single female can produce a litter of 3.9 pups [N_R_i = a litter of 3.9 pups], and under optimal conditions, she can average approximately 6.5 litters each year [F_R_i = approximately 6.5 litters each year] when maintained at 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. This high frequency of breeding events, when combined with the moderate litter size, yields a substantial total annual reproductive output. The short gestation period of 23 days [tg = 23 days] at a stable temperature of 35.3 °C [T = 35.3 °C] is a critical enabler of this rapid cycling, allowing females to return to estrus and conceive again almost immediately after parturition. Post-partum estrus is common in this species, meaning a female can be simultaneously lactating one litter while gestating the next. This strategy of overlapping reproductive events is a powerful demographic tool, allowing populations to increase their numbers rapidly when rainfall triggers a pulse of primary productivity and seed availability in their arid habitat.

Adult female Cape gerbils eventually attain a definitive, asymptotic body mass. In captivity, ultimate wet weight for females reaches a maximum of 106.5 grams [Wwi = 106.5 grams], though field studies and aging databases often report a lower average, around 74.8 grams, suggesting environmental constraints on growth in the wild. This variability in adult body size is common in gerbils and is likely influenced by seasonal food availability and local population density. At the physiological level, a major component of the species' energetic budget is its basal oxygen consumption. Respirometry trials have measured a maximal resting metabolic rate of 182.1 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 182.1 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when the animal is at its thermoneutral zone of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This metabolic rate is a fundamental metric that underpins all other life processes, from foraging activity to growth and reproduction. It reflects the cost of maintaining homeostasis in a thermally labile environment, where daytime burrow temperatures can fluctuate significantly.

Despite their prodigious reproductive capacity, Cape gerbils are not immune to the forces of mortality and senescence. The maximum documented lifespan for this species, recorded in captive individuals maintained at the optimal temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], is approximately 5.7 years [am = approximately 5.7 years], which equates to just over 2000 days of life. This longevity is relatively high for a rodent of its size, a trait often associated with species that have evolved bet-hedging life-history strategies in variable environments. The combination of a high maximum lifespan with elevated reproductive rates presents an interesting demographic profile, suggesting that while the species can boom under good conditions, adult survival during harsh periods is also sufficient to sustain the population through bottlenecks. Natural mortality in the wild is primarily driven by predation from raptors, snakes, and small carnivores, as well as by extreme climatic events. The ultimate limit of the species' life history is thus a product of its intrinsic physiological ceiling and the extrinsic hazards of its South African landscape.
